title: Introduction: Static Batching and Wasted GPU Compute
text: Hi, I am Simba. Say a batch of eight requests starts decoding together. One of them finishes after 20 tokens. Another needs 400. Static batching holds all eight slots until the slowest one is done. So, for the last few hundred tokens, most of those slots are doing nothing useful. What if a finished slot could just be handed to the next request waiting in line? Here's the idea. After every single decoding step, a scheduler looks at the batch. Static batching, the baseline, eight requests start together and the batch doesn't release until every single one is done. The ones that finish early don't leave. They sit there, padded, holding a slot for nothing, while new requests queue outside and wait for the whole group to drain. Two ways to run a batch. Static, a fixed group for its whole lifetime, a finished sequence still takes up a slot, padded, and new requests wait for every slot to clear. Continuous, the scheduler redecides who's in the batch every single step. A finished sequence is evicted right away and a new request can join on the next one. Mechanically, it's a loop. Whether anything just hit its end token or its length limit. If something finished, evict it, free the slot, and pull the next request off the queue into that slot. Whatever the batch looks like now, decode one more step and check again. The batch's membership is a decision made fresh every single step. Here's a small worked example. Four slots. Request B finishes at step three, a short request. Slot two doesn't sit idle. Request C gets admitted right at step four, starting with its own profile step while the others keep decoding. Slot four stays empty until step six, not because the scheduler is slow, but because the queue was actually empty until then. Continuous batching fills a slot the moment there's something to fill it with, nothing more. This only works cheaply if the KV cache is managed per sequence, allocated and freed

And how a new request's first step gets handled. Prefill is a heavier, more compute-bound step than an ongoing decode, so admitting several requests at once can spike that step's cost. What actually caps the gain isn't the scheduling idea, it's memory. A clever scheduler staring at a full KV cache still has nowhere to put a new request. And every admission mixes a prefill step into what was a steady decode pattern. That changes the cost of the step itself, not just how many slots are filled. The tradeoff is real. title: Engineering Trade-offs: Latency Dependencies and Memory Limits
text: Start. You take on a scheduling decision every single step instead of one decision at the start, and your latency now depends partly on who else happened to get admitted around you. So, continuous batching reclaims the GPU time static batching spends on padded, already finished slots by redesigning the batch every step instead of once. What it costs is a scheduler running continuously and KV cache memory managed per sequence to make that cheap. And it's worth saying plainly what it isn't. It's not a way around a full cache.
